sentences.text: This crocodylomorph is distinguished by laterally bulged snout edges, a feature most prominent near an enlarged maxillary tooth.
The species A. rattoides possessed a highly enlarged, forward-pointing first dentary tooth called an incisiform, resembling rodent incisors.
Araripesuchus had thin osteoderms covering its entire body, including multiple rows across the back and paired rows along the tail.
While one skull measures 130 millimeters, making it the largest Araripesuchus skull known, this specific measurement refers to the species A. buitreraensis.
A. wegeneri is estimated to have reached 81 cm in length, while A. rattoides could reach up to 1 meter.
Evidence from lines of arrested growth in its bones shows that this animal grew slowly with annual interruptions.
The genus Araripesuchus was named in 1959 based on fossils from the Santana Group in Brazil, originally described as A. gomesii from the Santana Formation.
The holotype specimen 423-R, consisting of a single skull articulated with part of a lower jaw, is housed in Rio de Janeiro.
The species A. wegeneri was described in 1981 from Early Cretaceous deposits in Niger, Africa, where it was found in Lower Cretaceous strata.
A third species, A. tsangatsangana, was described in 2006 from Late Cretaceous deposits on the island of Madagascar.
A fourth species, A. patagonicus, was described in 2000 from a specimen found in Patagonia, Argentina.
Araripesuchus likely spent more time on land than in water, suggested by its non-keeled osteoderms, long limb bones, and upright posture.
Araripesuchus is generally classified as a notosuchian within the clade Mesoeucrocodylia.
Recent phylogenetic analyses generally place Araripesuchus as a basal notosuchian, though some studies suggest it is more closely related to the Neosuchia clade.
The genus was originally assigned to the family Uruguaysuchidae by Price in 1959, and a 2011 analysis by Soto et al. united Araripesuchus with Uruguaysuchus to re-establish that family.
In 2000, Ortega et al. and other studies placed Araripesuchus outside of Notosuchia following the description of A. patagonicus.
There are currently seven recognized species within the genus Araripesuchus.
Araripesuchus lived during the Cretaceous period, approximately 125 to 66 million years ago, specifically from the Aptian to the Maastrichtian, between 121.4 and 66 million years ago.
Fossils found in South America and Africa suggest a Gondwanan origin for Araripesuchus, indicating a Gondwanan origin for the evolution of the genus.
Some recent analyses question the validity of the genus Araripesuchus by placing A. wegeneri as a sister taxon to Anatosuchus.
